full_judgment:
9. After conclusion of evidence, the accused Abdul Majid was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and his statement was recorded. Defence plea was of innocence and false implication. Defence adduced no evidence. 

 10. Upon consideration of the evidence on record, the trial Court found accused Abdul Majid guilty under section 364 of the Penal Code and accordingly, convicted and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10 (ten) years and to pay a fine of Taka 2,000 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1 (one) year more vide judgment dated 8-8-2000. 

 13. The learned Counsel next submits that the victim had been missing since 19-2-98 i.e. the alleged date of occurrence, and after 5 days a GD was filed bythe father of the victim, i.e. by PW 1 the present informant, being GD No. 917 dated 24-2-98 wherein nothing was mentioned against the appellant who was not even suspected therein, although before filing of the said GD PWs 2,3,4,5, 7 and 8 met with the informant to inform him about their seeing the victim with accused Abdul Majid going together in a van towards the Domar Bazar Subsequently, after one month of the missing of victim Shefali Begum, PW 1 filed petition of complaint on 19-3-98 wherein he brought a totally new case of abduction of his daughter by accused appellant, which was nothing but the product of after-thought and a concocted story. According to the learned lawyer the said GD which was the earliest information relating to the missing of the victim, was not produced at the trial to be marked as an Exhibit. Non production of the same prejudiced the appellant and thus the appellant would been titled to get the benefit under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, because if the GD was produced before the court, it would falsify the prosecution case. In support of his contention, he refers to the decisions as reported in 28 DLR 192 and 39 DLR (AD) 166. 

 14. Learned Advocate shows from the evidence of witnesses on record, the discrepancies and amomalies as to the seeing of the victim together with appellant just before her missing. He pointed out that PW 3 deposed that the victim was seen alone going through the Bazar in a van while other witnesses deposed that they saw the victim Shefali Begum and accused Majid going together in a van along with 2/3 others. All the prosecution witnesses who saw Shefali in the van informed PW 1 about it but no such allegation was disclosed in the petition of complaint as well as in the GD as stated above Learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the GD was intentionally withheld during trial in order to conceal what was stated therein as to the occurrence. He submits that the said GD being earliest in point of time will be first information report according to law and subsequent first information report will have value not more than the statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 15. He argues that victim who earlier got married 4 times with different persons was a woman of questionable character and, as such, she might have gone away with someone else of her choice. There is nothing on record to show that she was abducted or kidnapped by the appellant for the purpose of murder or to be put in danger of being murdered and thus the ingredients of section 364 of the Penal Code will be totally absent in the case. He also submits that the mere fact that the victim and the appellant were last seen together just before missing cannot lead to the conclusion that she was abducted by the appellant. He further submits that there is no evidence or allegation that the victim was murdered. Since it is not a wife killing case, the principle will not be applicable as laid down by superior courts in several cases to the effect that the husband will have to discharge obligation or to explain as to how his wife meets the end of her life while living with him in his house and custody and failure to discharge such obligation, the husband will be held liable for the death of his wife. Referring to the decisions reported in 11 DLR (SC) 365, 16 DLR (SC) 261, 1986 BLD (AD) 1, 38 DLR (AD) 311, the learned Advocate submits that there is distinction between a case where a person has been murdered after abduction and the case where a person has only been abducted without any proof of murder and no dead body being recovered. He finally submits that the prosecution miserably failed to prove the charge beyond all reasonable doubt against accused appellant Abdul Majid and, as such, impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence must be set aside and the appeal must succeed. 

 18. We have considered the submissions of both the parties, perused the evidence on record and scrutinised the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 19. Admittedly Shefali was the married wife of accused appellant Abdul Majid and they lived together as husband and wife in the same house just before the occurrence. It was disclosed that accused appellant Abdul Majid had earlier wife and children. Naturally, the marriage of victim by appellant Abdul Majid was not viewed well by the 1st wife and children. It was also disclosed that appellant Abdul Majid had to live in separate house with victim for the above reason. It is in evidence that PW 2 Sheuli was the daughter of victim Shefali by her former husband. PW 2 Sheuli stated in her deposition that she used to stay with her mother, the victim, during day time and at night she used to stay in the house of her grandfather (informant PW 1). PW 2 stated clearly that on 19-2-98 (Thursday) her step-father (accused appellant Abdul. Majid) took her mother (victim) in a van towards bazar. She wanted to go with them but they did not take her with them. 

 27. In view of evidence of PW 1, it appears that appellant Abdul Majid told PW 1 that he sent Shefali to Dhaka. But PW 1 got no truth of such version of appellant Abdul Majid who was bound to say about exact location of his wife Shefali. Therefore, we presume that appellant Abdul Majid gave false information to PW 1 as to sending Shefali to Dhaka. In above context the decisions in the wife killing cases will be equally applicable to the present wife missing case also inasmuch as in both types of cases the husband will be saddled with the obligation to explain as to how his married wife while living in his house and custody had met with death or had been missing from his custody. For argument's sake, even if we exclude the evidence of PWs 2-5, 7 and 8 as above from our consideration then also above positive circumstances will show that just before occurrence as to missing of victim Shefali, she was in the house of appellant Abdul Majid as his married wife. It will give rise to strong circumstances that appellant Abdul Majid alone will be liable for the missing of his wife as he failed to discharge his obligation properly to explain as to what has happened to his married wife Shefali who lived in his house and custody just before her missing. 

 32. We have given anxious consideration to above facts and circumstances. We are of the view that we cannot safely rely on the evidence adduced at the trial to reach correct decision. But in this case there are so much strong, unavoidable and reliable circumstances which positively indicate the probable involvement of the accused appellant Abdul Majid and show his complicity in the matter as to the missing or intractability of the victim Shefali being the admitted married wife of the appellant from his house and custody. 

 33. We noticed above that just before occurrence as to missing of the victim Shefali she as married wife of accused appellant Abdul Majid had been in the house and custody of the appellant. If the victim be untraceable from the house and custody of the appellant, her husband, natural and usual obligation will lie upon the husband to explain what has happened to the wife, or where she has gone to or where she has been sent to. The accused appellant appears to have not at all discharged his above obligation as a husband and did not try to find out the whereabouts of his wife after her missing from his house. It appears from evidence of PW 1, the informant, Merajuddin that accused appellant gave him the news that he sent the victim to Dhaka, but such plea or pretext of the appellant was found to be untrue and false. Thereafter, accused appellant remained absconding with guilty mind having knowledge indicating that he had complicity in the matter as to the non-availability of the victim as his wife. The accused appellant at no stage of the proceeding did anything to expose or express his anxiety or reaction about the missing of the victim, as his married wife, from his house and custody.
